details:
**David Hume**
The Scottish empiricist philosopher who wrote this work, first published in 1748. He wrote it as a shorter, more readable version of the ideas in Book 1 of his earlier A Treatise of Human Nature, which had sold poorly.

**"Relations of ideas" and "matters of fact" (Hume's fork)**
The work's central distinction. Relations of ideas, like the truths of math, can be known with certainty by reason alone, while matters of fact, like "the sun will rise tomorrow," can only be known through experience, and their denial is not a contradiction. This division is known as "Hume's fork."

**Missing shade of blue**
A possible counterexample that Hume raises against his own theory. A person who has seen every shade of blue except one could probably imagine the missing shade without ever having had an impression of it. Hume admits the case but dismisses it as too unusual to change his general principle.

**"Of Miracles"**
Section X of the work, which defines a miracle as a "violation of the laws of nature." Hume argues that the uniform experience behind a law of nature will always outweigh human testimony that a miracle happened, so a wise person should never believe such reports.

**Problem of induction**
Hume asks what justifies inductive inferences, such as expecting the future to resemble the past. He concludes that such reasoning cannot be justified by reason or experience without circularity, and that it rests on custom or habit. This casts doubt on how far scientific claims can be trusted.

**"Of the Origin of Ideas" (impressions and ideas)**
Section II, where Hume divides perceptions into impressions (vivid sensations and feelings) and ideas (faint copies of them). He argues that ideas lack the force and liveliness of impressions and that every simple idea ultimately comes from an impression.

**"Of Probability"**
Section VI, which argues that there is no real chance in the universe. What people call chance or luck is just ignorance of the real causes of events, and belief in an outcome grows stronger as more possible cases favor it.

**Custom and necessary connection**
In the sections on cause and effect and "Of the Idea of Necessary Connexion," Hume argues that we never observe a necessary link between a cause and its effect, only one event regularly following another. Our idea of necessity comes from the mind's habit of expecting the effect after seeing the cause.

**Billiard balls**
Hume's famous example of causation. When one billiard ball strikes another, we see only one motion followed by another and never the "power" that connects them, so the effect could not be predicted before experience.

**"Commit it then to the flames"**
The famous ending of Section XII. Hume says that if a book contains no abstract reasoning about quantity or number and no experimental reasoning about matters of fact, it should be burned, because it can contain "nothing but sophistry and illusion."

**John Locke and empiricism**
The Enquiry is a key text of British empiricism, the view that all knowledge comes from experience. It builds on the work of John Locke, whose An Essay Concerning Human Understanding has a similar title.

**"Of Liberty and Necessity"**
Section VIII, where Hume offers a compatibilist answer to the free will debate. He argues that human actions are caused like everything else, but that this necessity is consistent with liberty, meaning the power to act according to one's own will.
